articles.title: The 'rising star' of the whisky industry at Annandale Distillery
articles.summary: Zoey Darnbrough had no idea there was a distillery near her home - now she has a top tourism role there.
articles.body:
Zoey Darnbrough is the first to admit that just a few years ago she did not even know there was a whisky distillery near her hometown in southern Scotland.

But it hasn't stopped her rising rapidly from tour guide, to group tourism and events co-ordinator at the site near Annan.

She went away to study heritage and tourism in Stirling after school, but unlike many of her peers, she returned to Dumfries and Galloway for work.

Now she hopes to play her part in changing people's opinions of the world of whisky "one woman at a time".

The 26-year-old, who attended St Joseph's College in Dumfries, was recently nominated for "rising star" recognition at the South of Scotland Thistle Awards.

Zoey said her journey had not been straightforward as she did not get the exam results she had hoped for at school, so she spent time working in the kitchens at Dumfries Infirmary.

But when a job came up at Annandale Distillery, she jumped at the chance.

She said: "My first thought was - there's a distillery in Annan? And my second thought was - whisky?

"I thought I'd give it a chance and see what it was like because there's a lot of heritage when it comes to whisky.

"And I've now been here three-and-a-half years and I've not looked back."

Revived distillery toasts first 10-year-old malt

What does she think the area has to offer that others her age might ignore?

One thing she highlighted was the relative costs of property compared with city prices.

Zoey also believes the area has a lot to shout about and is happy to have returned after university.

"The south of Scotland has so much heritage and it is a passion of mine," she said.

"So I would naturally like to be somewhere where there's a lot of heritage and where I can kind of grow as an individual."

But she agrees that a lot more could be done to stop young people from leaving.

"I would like to think we could go back to the local schools across the region and try and explain that there are other careers out there including in heritage and tourism," she said.

Zoey would also like to see the area market itself better.

"We've got so much to offer in terms of castles, in terms of scenery, in terms of attractions, accommodation, it's so vast," she said.

"I always like to say that we've got everything that the Highlands have, but just in a much quieter area.

"But we're going to use that quietness to our strength."

She has certainly achieved that in her own career in the whisky industry - despite some people assuming she might lack the knowledge of older, male counterparts.

"It has been tricky, I'm not going to lie," she said. "But I always think that if you prepare yourself well, those types of questions cannot faze you.

"I've been so fortunate that all my experiences have been mostly pleasant and so I have not really felt it, but I do understand the struggles that other people face.

"We just need to start changing people's opinions one woman at a time."

Zoey is happy to do that from Dumfries and Galloway for the foreseeable future.

"I'm only beginning to stick my teeth into the south of Scotland," she said. "So to leave, it would have to be a fairly big jump."

articles.title: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise UK coastal towns?
articles.summary: Engineer David Mummery has developed a tidal energy generator that he says can change lives for people living in coastal communities.
articles.body:
In a secret location in the Highlands of Scotland, there's a fast-flowing river that's the key to understanding the massive power of water.

It's where engineer David Mummery found himself more than a decade ago.

With a length of cord tied tightly across the river, he swam out, gripped firmly, and let the unstoppable current rush over as he sunk his head below the surface.

"As an engineer we do the maths and stuff," he says, "but sometimes you can get a lot more from actually touching the water and feeling it".

As he lay down in the powerful rapids, he visualised a new type of small-scale tidal energy generator.

It's an innovation he says could change lives for people in coastal communities.

"I'd be under the river, feeling the turbulence of the water rushing over me.

"Trying to envisage how this turbine needed to interact with that environment - to understand the way the water was working."

Mummery's idea became the Swimmer Turbine - a 50kw tidal generator named after his experience in the river.

Anchored to the sea floor, the fiberglass and steel device lies invisible below the water's surface. It can generate enough electricity to power about 30 homes.

He began tests in the river in early 2010s. On a patent lawyer's advice he found a secret location, far from curious Highland tourists and their cameras.

"You're trying to be quite discreet because you're working with new technology," he says.

It was in the first years of his company, Flex Marine Power, long before Britain was gripped by the soaring costs of an energy crisis.

The size of the Swimmer Turbine is what sets it apart from large tidal projects dotted around Scottish waters.

Scotland is a world leader in the sector at sites including:

Nova Innovation - The world's first tidal stream array, deployed in 2016 in Bluemull Sound in Shetland

MeyGen - The world's largest tidal array, with four large 1.5MW turbines on the seabed of the Pentland Firth

Orbital O2 - The world's most powerful floating turbine, generating 2MW, anchored at Fall of Warness in the Orkney Islands

Mummery's turbine is ultra compact and low cost compared to these giant machines. Fishermen and local workers can build and install it themselves from their own village harbour.

"Can you imagine like an Ikea furniture kit? You get a shipping container and you'll open it up and it will be about 20 components.

"You'll bolt them all together and then you've got your turbine ready.

"There'll be a launch plan, you follow these instructions, then you'll be in the water."

Mummery's work did not always focus on small-scale power. Originally from Guildford, he studied mechanical engineering at Surrey University.

Before founding Flex Marine Power, he was a sought-after consultant in the UK energy sector. For a time he specialised in nuclear work and decommissioning, designing robots for pulling material out of contaminated tanks.

He moved north after falling in love with a girl studying at Glasgow University. Jo became his wife and they now live in the city suburbs with three young children.

Conveniently, Mummery's relocation came at a time when Scotland was establishing its reputation as a centre for marine power expertise.

In 2010 he took a secondment at Scottish Power Renewables on the ground-breaking Pelamis project in Orkney.

The 180m-long (591ft) Pelamis P2 - nicknamed the sea snake - was the first deep-water, floating wave energy machine to generate power for the national grid.

Ultimately, Pelamis went into administration in 2014 , but the ill-fated device remains celebrated as a milestone in marine power innovation.

"The industry is littered with these examples of fantastic technologies and teams that do brave things that take decades," Mummery says.

"But at some point the market doesn't step up and they falter. Some really good ones have lasted the course, but others have not and it's sad."

Mummery says the UK has "phenomenal waters for tidal power" and he loved being a part of major projects - but couldn't shake a discomfort.

His work felt incongruous to the many small coastal communities he found himself in.

"I'd be going out on boats around Scotland doing sonar surveys with all these really expensive pieces of kit.

"But the equipment was all really big, utility-scale stuff that would weigh hundreds of tonnes, shipped by people from the mainland.

"All the people I was meeting in harbours or in the pub were fishermen. And they were knowledgeable and they were interested.

"I thought 'we've got to do this in a way that they can take the lead'."

That, he says, is what motivated his Swimmer Turbine idea.

In 2011 he left big projects behind to found Flex Marine Power and focus on his turbine concept.

He spent hours at his desk sketching, working out how to make the technology smaller and lighter.

He hired a student employee and found a sleek, glass office space outside Glasgow - which he quickly discovered wasn't entirely suited to an engineer and his tools.

"It was a lovely place, but I wasn't allowed to take a hammer drill into the office.

"We were trying to make prototype turbines under the desk so the landlord wouldn't see them when he came in."

Mummery turned to Clydeside's shipbuilding past in search of a more suitable workspace.

He presented a plan to convert former shipyards for marine technology research, and was invited to Greenock by Inverclyde's redevelopment authority.

"There were lots of empty sheds that hadn't been used for years," he says.

"They basically said 'we'll walk you around, you can pick a shed'. So I got the pick of the bunch right on the quayside."

Mummery now had direct access to the River Clyde for sea trials to test his models.

He developed a prototype which he successfully trialled in 2015 on the island of Luing, in the Firth of Lorn, near Oban.

It secured Flex Marine's first major investment and expansion the following year.

The next major step was in Northern Ireland in 2020, at Strangford Narrows in County Down.

Mummery worked with Queen's University Belfast who had an academic license to test tidal equipment at sea.

"Me and Mark, my accountant, lifted all of the components into a shipping container and sent it out on a lorry.

"We were introduced to a bunch of local mariners. We pulled off a full-scale tidal turbine installation out of a container deposited in a farmyard."

Generating electricity while tethered to the back of a boat, Mummery says it was the full-scale proof-of-concept that "finally put us on the map".

It helped Flex Marine Power secure £968,000 from the UK government's Energy Entrepreneurs Fund for a team of nine people to develop a commercial turbine model.

This version would not be tied to a boat.

The Swimmer Turbine would launch directly from shore and remain absolutely hidden, generating electricity below the surface of the water.

Mummery took it through months of testing last year on the island of Islay - famous for its many whisky distilleries and coastal waters that are perfect for tidal power.

He rented space at a boatyard where "talented local people" were taught how to assemble and launch the device.

Finally, after his years of work, came the defining moment.

"I was standing at the end of the slipway, seeing our machine, without any of my guys touching it.

"It was all local people. Fishermen, using their own tractor, launching it down their own slipway. This was my vision in a nutshell."

The next stage is putting the power to good use. Mummery will return to Islay next year with a plan to generate electricity for the island.

"The sea is a very big space and these things are invisible. There could be different tidal arrays in different parts of the island, all owned by different people.

"In those real coastal communities, they don't have flashy cranes and heavy lifting capabilities and big corporate companies with big pockets.

"But what they do have is knowledge and work ethic and a deep understanding of their environment and the sea.

"We're trying to equip real people to thrive by giving them access to the power that's in the tides."

Wave tech 'belongs in a museum not a scrapyard'

articles.title: 'Urgent shopping' amid chaos: 1,200 arrested, 150 police hurt as France stores looted, vandalised
articles.summary: What began as a collective expression of frustration in France has now left even those caught in the same struggle standing on opposite sides.
articles.body: What began as a collective expression of frustration in France has now left even those caught in the same struggle standing on opposite sides. Looters smashed shop windows, ransacked stores and attacked shopkeepers in Paris on Saturday as protests over the cost of living descended into violence across France. Videos circulating on social media captured the unrest, showing people being handled by the crowd after objecting to looting and vandalising shops.In one video, a French woman who had joined the protests shouted, “This isn’t the cause” as other demonstrators began looting stores. The protesters then could be seen pushing her aside, telling her to shut up and claiming they had “urgent shopping” to do.Another video showed a man getting hit by protesters after an attempt to protect his shop. The shopkeeper could be seen getting mocked and beaten as his business was vandalised. The footage drew harsh reactions online, with one post describing the attackers as “terrorists” and saying, “Europe is dying.”French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers injured as the unrest spread. Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and set off fireworks.The violence erupted on the sidelines of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs, drawing hundreds of thousands of people and adding to political uncertainty ahead of France's presidential election in six months.Looters strip shops of goodsIn Paris, masked men wearing black hoodies forced open metal shutters and cleared shelves of cigarettes, sunglasses, clothes, jewellery and food. Looters have been leaving supermarkets with bags filled with cakes, fruit juice and alcohol, according to a report by news agency AFP.A jewellery shop across the street was targeted for its antique clocks, while entire display racks of sunglasses disappeared from a street corner.Inside the stores, looters searched for cash registers and smashed them on the floor, sometimes discovering that they were empty.The destruction left streets littered with broken glass and debris. Near the iconic Place de la République in central Paris, burning vehicle can be seen sending thick smoke into the air.'They must have some pretty deep anger'The scenes of destruction unfolded alongside an unusual contrast in the capital, where restaurants, hotels and residential buildings were largely spared. Some Parisians continued their usual Saturday lunches as looters wreaked havoc on nearby streets, while others watched from their apartments.Perched on a pavement terrace with a colleague, 38-year-old art teacher Alma said she had “never seen anything like it”.Alma and her companion had joined an unsuccessful march earlier in the day to reach the French president's residence, the Élysée Palace. Despite the violence, they said they “understand” the revolt.“I understand why people might be upset, but I think damaging property is fine, as long as we don't physically harm anyone,” Alma said.Jules, a 29-year-old civil servant, watched the unrest from a safe distance.“What a sight,” he said, “They must have some pretty deep anger. They're a part of society who doesn't feel integrated.”While acknowledging the right to protest, Jules said the looters were “undermining their own goals”.“Just look at the state of the street,” he said as quoted by AFP.Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said entire streets “have been devastated” by the violence. He distinguished between the “fundamental” right to protest and what he called “unacceptable” violence.Conflicting estimates of protest turnoutThe unrest followed demonstrations against rising living costs, which came after weeks of student protests and heightened political uncertainty.France's interior ministry estimated that 550,000 people had taken part in marches across the country. The CGT union, which participated in the demonstrations, put the figure at 800,000.Police confronted protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers. The clashes left dozens of police officers injured and prompted mass arrests.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: In 2008, a woman bought a glass vase for just £1 at a car-boot sale in Dumfries, Scotland, because she liked how it looked.
articles.body: In 2008, a woman bought a glass vase for just £1 at a car-boot sale in Dumfries, Scotland, because she liked how it looked. She used it as a plant pot without knowing that it was a rare piece by French glass designer René Lalique. Later that year, the vase was identified as a valuable 1929 Lalique creation and sold at Christie’s auction house in London for £32,450. articles.title: Jennifer Lopez’s family foundation donated telemedicine equipment in 2012; a seven-centre network in Panama connected children’s doctors with specialists at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles
articles.summary: Singer Jennifer Lopez and her sister, Lynda Lopez, have helped expand access to specialist medical care for children in Panama through a donation of
articles.body: Singer Jennifer Lopez and her sister, Lynda Lopez, have helped expand access to specialist medical care for children in Panama through a donation of telemedicine equipment. In 2012, their Lopez Family Foundation supported a network linking hospitals and health centres in Panama with Children's Hospital Los Angeles in the United States. The system allowed doctors to examine medical information, discuss diagnoses and seek specialist advice remotely, particularly for children living in areas where specialised healthcare was difficult to access.According to Panama's Spanish newspaper La Prensa, for families in the country's remote Ngabe-Bugle indigenous region, reaching a hospital with specialist doctors could involve travelling considerable distances. With the new programme, a child could be examined at a participating healthcare facility while doctors elsewhere reviewed the findings and helped decide what treatment or further attention was needed.The initiative had taken shape the previous year, when Lynda Lopez and Dr Stuart Siegel of Children's Hospital Los Angeles visited hospitals and communities in the country. On June 12, 2012, the Lopez sisters visited Hospital del Nino to hand over the donated equipment. Panama became the second country to receive the programme after Puerto Rico.How doctors could examine patients from another hospitalThe programme was designed around an existing healthcare network rather than requiring every hospital to have its own team of specialists. Hospital del Nino in Panama City served as the coordinating centre, while other participating facilities could request medical opinions according to their patients' needs.The donated equipment included three telemedicine units and seven tele-education units. Each telemedicine unit had a computer with medical software called t-consult, a stethoscope, an otoscope, a vital signs monitor, and an electrocardiograph. These devices allowed medical information collected during examinations to be shared with doctors at another location.The tele-education units were also equipped with computers, high-resolution cameras, communication software, and external speakers. This allowed healthcare workers to attend lectures, discuss cases and participate in training without travelling to another hospital.The original network connected four hospitals and three health centres. These included Hospital del Nino, Jose Domingo De Obaldia Hospital, San Felix Rural Hospital, the Paediatric Specialities Hospital and health centres at Hato Juli, Hato Chami and Cerro Iglesias. Participating hospitals could also consult specialists in Los Angeles.Use of telemedicine in PanamaThe Lopez Family Foundation's contribution built upon medical services that had existed in Panama for more than a decade. Telemedicine activities began in the country in 1999, followed by a rural project in the Ngabe-Bugle region in 2005.That earlier project enabled healthcare workers in mountainous communities to contact specialists at San Felix Rural Hospital. However, patients requiring more specialised treatment were generally referred to Jose Domingo De Obaldia Hospital.The new network was intended to improve communication between these facilities and provide access to additional expertise. Panamanian pathologist Silvio Vega, who directed the programme locally, helped oversee its installation and development.For patients, this meant fewer unnecessary hospital transfers, lower travel expenses and better access to follow-up consultations. For doctors, the system offered an opportunity to obtain second opinions while continuing to care for children at their local facilities.Network also supported medical educationThe programme subsequently developed into a platform for sharing medical knowledge. According to Hospital del Nino's official account, its first telepediatrics conference addressed growth disorders in children. The session was led by Dr Mitchell Geffner, head of Endocrinology and Metabolism at Children's Hospital Los Angeles, with doctors from several participating hospitals joining remotely.Training also extended beyond video conferences. In 2013, Dr Rebeca Rios Zavala completed a month-long placement at Children's Hospital Los Angeles. Three paediatric residents from Los Angeles subsequently visited hospitals in Panama during in 2014 to learn more about tropical diseases.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Unacceptable’: Chirag Paswan slams Imran Khan’s role in Mumbai protests, backs ‘Leave India’ notice
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Sunday reacted to the ‘Leave India’ notice issued to actor Imran Khan over his participation in protests
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Sunday reacted to the ‘Leave India’ notice issued to actor Imran Khan over his participation in protests seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Paswan termed the involvement of foreign nationals in India’s internal affairs “unacceptable”, while expressing support for peaceful protests by Indian citizens.“There is no objection to Indian citizens playing a role in matters concerning India while living within the country. I have always supported peaceful protests. However, I do not consider it justifiable for someone who is not an Indian citizen to intervene in India's internal affairs or play a role in such matters,” he told news agency ANI.“For someone who is not an Indian citizen to involve themselves in India's internal affairs—especially when there are growing concerns that foreign forces may be involved in orchestrating these events—is unacceptable,” the Union minister added.Paswan’s remarks follow the issuance of a ‘Leave India’ notice to Imran Khan by Mumbai Police on Thursday. The notice directs the actor to leave India by October 28. According to ANI, Khan, the nephew of actor Aamir Khan, holds an American passport.Authorities have initiated action against him under Sections 29 and 7 of the Immigration Act over allegations that he participated in a protest despite not being an Indian citizen.Khan had joined a demonstration at Mumbai’s August Kranti Maidan, where protesters demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. He was detained by Mumbai Police last week.After his detention, the actor posted a picture of himself apparently sitting inside a police van, with the caption, “Apparently I’m going for a drive.”Khan said he had visited the protest site as a citizen of Mumbai and was not there to press any specific demands. He also raised questions about freedom of movement and what he described as the suppression of people’s voices.On Saturday, Khan approached the Bombay high court, challenging the notice issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) over alleged violations of the Foreigners Act. His lawyer indicated that the notice would be contested in court.Earlier, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Kirit Somaiya had called for Khan’s immediate arrest and deportation, alleging violations of Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) provisions and visa conditions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
articles.summary: The flying instructor has been described as "a gentleman and an experienced aviator" by former students.
articles.body:
An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis.

He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released.

The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.

Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.

Tributes posted on social media by former students describe the flying instructor as "a gentleman and an experienced aviator", and a "good friend".

The plane - a Piper Tomahawk II aircraft - is registered to Leading Edge Flight Training in Renfrew, according to the Civil Aviation Authority's aircraft register.

Previous social media posts on Leading Edge's Facebook page report the instructor's nickname as the 'Flying Haggis', and show that he had been working with the flying school.

BBC Scotland has approached Leading Edge Flight Training for comment.

Gavin Birch-Williams, managing director of Glasgow Airport, said: "We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow Airport.

"This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow Airport are with the friends and families affected."

The plane had earlier taken off from Cumbernauld Airport at 11:46, before flying 15 minutes to Glasgow Airport.

It stayed there until about 13:00, before doing a two-hour flight north east to Newport-on-Tay then turning round and heading back to Glasgow.

It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and started its final flight.

articles.title: ‘My rhetoric has been imperfect’: JD Vance walks back H-1B ‘indentured servants’ remark after India’s protest
articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has acknowledged that his rhetoric was “imperfect” after describing foreign professionals working on H-1B visas as “indentured
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has acknowledged that his rhetoric was “imperfect” after describing foreign professionals working on H-1B visas as “indentured servants”, clarifying that his criticism was directed at American companies and the visa system rather than the workers themselves.Speaking at a CBS News town hall on Saturday, Vance said he took responsibility for his choice of words following criticism, including from India, which had described the terminology as “deeply offensive” and said it carried painful historical and colonial legacy connotations.“I would say, and to the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me,” Vance said in response to a question from an Indian immigrant who became a US citizen five years ago and voted for President Donald Trump.Vance argued that the H-1B visa system could leave foreign employees vulnerable because their legal status in the United States is closely tied to their employment. He said employers could exercise excessive control over workers who risk losing their ability to remain in the country if they lose their jobs.The Vice President said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder."He explained that companies sponsoring H-1B workers certify that they cannot find an alternative American applicant for the position, while the workers’ visas often serve as their “only lifeline to the United States of America”.“So, when I say indentured servitude, that is not a criticism of H1B visa holders; that is the criticism of the company, which brings a person who sometimes will lay off an American worker and knows that if they complain, if they have disagreement with the boss, they could just lose their job… They can be shipped back, which I think gives way too much power to the employer. Maybe my rhetoric has been imperfect here… it is the criticism of the visa system that allowed people to be treated as indentured servants, as they can be shipped to their countries of origin,” Vance added.Vance says he does not intend to dehumanise immigrantsVance also referred to his own family while explaining his position on immigration, saying the United States needed to balance welcoming foreign professionals with protecting American workers.“You know where my family comes from, and I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India, and obviously their daughter, born in the United States of America, is now the second lady, and I’m very proud of her, and I love her very much,” he said.His wife, Usha Vance, is the daughter of Indian immigrants.Acknowledging that he was not perfect, the Vice President said his intention was not to dehumanise people who had moved to the United States.“I will tell you that nobody's perfect, certainly not me. But my goal here is not to dehumanise any immigrant, and in fact, I love a number of immigrants,” he said.India had called remarks ‘deeply offensive’Vance's clarification follows strong objections from ministry of external affairs (MEA), which had called his description of H-1B professionals “unwarranted” and said it overlooked their contributions to the American economy and innovation ecosystem.The ministry also highlighted the role generations of immigrants had played in the United States' growth and prosperity.“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the MEA said in its statement.It also emphasised that talent mobility benefits both countries by providing opportunities to Indian professionals while helping US companies access skilled workers and strengthen innovation, research, productivity and competitiveness.The MEA had clarified that the US decision to suspend certain companies from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme was separate from the H-1B visa programme.The suspension could affect the green card process for eligible employees of the companies concerned but did not, by itself, invalidate existing H-1B visas or change the status of visa holders and their dependants.Vance had accused firms of undercutting American wagesEarlier this month, Vance described H-1B workers as “indentured servants” and accused foreign outsourcing firms of bringing in employees at lower wages while laying off American workers.At a news conference on visa fraud, he claimed that H-1B workers earned $20,000 less than American citizens hired for similar positions. He further alleged that those brought in by foreign outsourcing firms earned $48,000 less than American workers in comparable roles.Vance also accused companies of profiting by replacing American employees with foreign workers paid lower wages.The Trump administration subsequently suspended eight companies — TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe — from participating in the PERM programme.PERM is an important step in the employment-based green card process. Employers generally need labour certification from the US Department of Labour before sponsoring eligible foreign workers for permanent residence.The process requires companies to establish that qualified, willing and available American workers cannot be found for the position and that employing a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.Indian professionals account for more than 70 per cent of approved H-1B petitions annually.You use AI every day. articles.title: France protests: Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
articles.summary: Around 1,800 people were arrested after nationwide protests saw outbreaks of violence and vandalism.
articles.body:
France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris.

Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful.

They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.

Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.

In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.

Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.

Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille, a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted.

More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured in the unrest on Saturday, France's interior ministry said.

Around 1,500 shops and retailers were also damaged in the disturbances, the Retail and Trade Federation said.

On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the aftermath, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace.

Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris.

Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich."

The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la République which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor.

The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process.

The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations.

Close to the Place de la République, a BBC reporter visited the Good Vibes bakery, whose glass front was completely shattered, and the Nicolas wine store, where every bottle was either stolen or smashed, leaving smell of alcohol lingering in the street.

CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves.

Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.

Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.

In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".

Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.

Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost."

"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.

Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media.

"Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said.

France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, and the western city of Angers.

Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.

articles.title: In 1977, Washington rebuilt a road using 72% old asphalt instead of new material; the recycled pavement lasted 16 years, compared with 10 years for the original road
articles.summary: Discover how Washington's innovative 1977 road project, using 72% recycled asphalt, outperformed traditional methods by lasting 16 years. Explore the benefits of pavement recycling in road construction and its implications for sustainability and cost savings!
articles.body: Road construction often involves removing worn-out pavement and replacing it with fresh materials. Old asphalt does not have to become waste, however. It can be processed and reused for road surfacing, which saves virgin materials for other uses. Washington State considered such an alternative in the 1970s, a period of rising construction costs and oil prices. A road rehabilitation project it carried out in 1977 produced notable results. The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) reported that the recycled hot-mix asphalt provided 16 years of actual service, compared with 10 years for the original layer it replaced.The 1977 project reused most of the existing asphaltThe Washington State Department of Transportation removed 45 mm of old pavement and laid recycled hot mix asphalt in its place. A thin open-graded friction course was then laid on top and FHWA’s archived documents give its thickness as either 18 or 20 millimetres. The recycled mix consisted of about 72% reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) and 0.75% recycling agent, with no new asphalt cement added. The agent’s application rate was selected to produce a recycled binder comparable to AR-4000W asphalt cement. These details appear in FHWA’s Performance Data of Recycled Mixtures. The project showed how a large proportion of existing pavement could be reused in a new road layer rather than discarded.Field tests examined the recycled asphalt's performanceThe project also tested asphalt binder retrieved from pavement cores taken over the following years, not just the condition of the road after reconstruction. The FHWA report said binder sampling took place over eight years. The average properties of the retrieved binder stayed within the limits for absolute viscosity and penetration during the first five years, which allowed the aged binder’s performance after recycling to be evaluated. The Washington State Department of Transportation also tested the resilient modulus of the recycled mixture and the results showed stiffness comparable to conventional hot-mix asphalt, both initially and over time. The service life comparison was the key finding. The recycled pavement gave 16 years of actual service, against 10 years for the original layer, so in this case the recycled mixture provided durable road construction.Oil prices helped drive interest in asphalt recyclingWashington’s project was one of many pavement recycling efforts in the United States. An oil embargo in the 1970s was one reason construction costs rose. FHWA’s Pavement Recycling Executive Summary and Reportexplains that the agency started Demonstration Project 39 in June 1976 to promote and assess asphalt pavement recycling. The programme helped establish that recycling was a technically viable way of rehabilitating roads.Reclaimed asphalt pavement is material produced by milling or removing existing asphalt pavement. It contains aggregate and aged asphalt binder and can be reused for paving, alone or combined with virgin aggregate, new binder, or a recycling agent. FHWA’s guidance identifies conserving materials, reducing waste and potential cost savings as benefits and stresses appropriate material selection, mixture design, processing and quality control.One project's results do not guarantee longer-lasting roadsThe Washington project illustrates how reclaimed asphalt can perform in road building. A pavement with a large share of reclaimed material and a recorded service life of 16 years shows that using existing pavement does not necessarily mean building a shorter-lived road. Nevertheless, the results cannot show that recycled asphalt lasts longer than newly produced asphalt. Pavement lifespan also depends on the condition of the reclaimed material, mixture quality, construction quality and environmental conditions. Reclaimed asphalt can become a real source of construction material if engineers evaluate it properly.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Roblox bets big on India: Company India MD Sunil Rao says ‘next big hit on Roblox could come from this country’
articles.summary: Roblox is putting its weight behind India’s creator community.
articles.body: Roblox is putting its weight behind India’s creator community. The gaming and creation platform held a familiarisation event called ‘UNBOX ROBLOX’ in New Delhi this week where it revisited the latest announcements from its developer conference, RDC 2026, along with showcasing new games and features for players, parents, creators and partners. Roblox also released an Economic Impact report for India, which it says shows its interest in investing in the country’s creator ecosystem. Sunil Rao, managing director of Roblox India and South Asia, highlighted the platform’s potential in the country, saying that “the next big hit could come from India.”“This is the age of small studios and the next big hit on Roblox could come from India. Roblox daily active users grew by 64% y-o-y* and I am excited about the possibilities that exist in this market across players, partners and creators,” he added. Roblox believes the platform can play a key role in growing both game consumption and creator careers in India. (*The growth figure is for the quarter ending June 30, 2026.)What Roblox offers creators in IndiaRao announced that Roblox will launch Build in India soon. It was first announced at RDC 2026. Additionally, Roblox launched in Hindi a few months ago, and more languages are coming soon. Moreover, creators can earn from their experiences through monetisation inside the app. Roblox Studio, a free to use service, helps people build experiences and also teaches design skills.Roblox India: What the numbers sayRoblox report highlights several figures about the company and India:India has more than 500 million gamers, the world’s second-largest gaming population. The report expects video game revenues to rise from Rs 6,300 crore in 2025 to Rs 9,200 crore by 2028. That is 13% annual growth, against 5.1% globally.Daily active users in India grew at a compound annual rate of 76% between 2020 and 2025, reaching millions of users.The number of Indian creators eligible for Roblox payouts grew at a compound annual rate of 96% over the same period, passing 250 in 2025. Total payouts grew 72% a year. Among surveyed creators who publish on several platforms, Roblox made up 61% of their creation revenue.About 94% of surveyed Indian creators say they can build games on Roblox with little prior experience, and 91% say its tools help them learn. On average, overseas players make up 52% of daily users and 55% of revenue on their games. The US, UK and Japan are the biggest export markets.About 91% of surveyed creators say their Roblox work helped them get job offers, freelance projects or business opportunities.Among surveyed Indian users, 88% play on mobile phones, 92% like learning at their own pace with free tutorials, 93% enjoy spending time with friends on the platform and 94% say it helps them unwind.Access Partnership estimates that creator activity added Rs 123.9 crore to India’s GDP between 2020 and 2025. articles.title: Jagan Mohan Reddy ‘regrets’ backing EC appointment bill in 2023, says democracy needs trusted institutions
articles.summary: VIJAYAWADA: Former chief minister YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has called for a rethink of the process of appointing Election Commissioners, saying recent reports
articles.body: VIJAYAWADA: Former chief minister YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has called for a rethink of the process of appointing Election Commissioners, saying recent reports of differences within the Election Commission have raised serious questions about the functioning of the electoral system. He suggested that the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, which his party had supported at the time, should be revisited. Jagan regretted backing the Bill in Parliament.Speaking to the media after meeting the State Election Commissioner (SEC), Jagan said democracy could function only when people had complete confidence in constitutional institutions such as the Election Commission. He said reports in the national media that two Election Commissioners had raised objections on several occasions over decisions, electoral rolls and the management of ECINet had led to doubts among the public.“Rather than an exchange of allegations, the public needs clarity on what objections were recorded, what action was taken on them, and how transparently the system functioned,” Jagan said.He said greater clarity was needed on the process of adding, deleting or restoring names in electoral rolls. “Steps are needed to give people confidence on these matters,” he said, adding that public trust in the electoral process must be strengthened and every citizen’s right to vote protected.Jagan said transparency should not only prevail but should also be seen to prevail in a democracy.He urged the Centre to amend the law and restore a three-member selection committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India for appointing Election Commissioners.Jagan said the appointment process should inspire confidence and be perceived as neutral. Citing the principle that a student appointing an examiner could invite allegations even if the examiner was completely honest, he argued that a neutral appointment mechanism would help restore the Election Commission’s standing and public confidence in the institution.He also alleged that the ruling party had misused its authority during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process in Andhra Pradesh and claimed that several appeals by his party had gone unheard.Referring to the local body elections, Jagan alleged that objections raised by the Opposition over the redrawing of divisions had also been brushed aside.“Such actions undoubtedly weaken public confidence in the electoral process,” he said. Jagan added that transparency and accountability were the true measures of an institution’s functioning in a democracy and that safeguarding them should be the Election Commission’s primary duty.Jagan said he had apprised the SEC of the situation in the state, alleging that candidates were not being allowed to file their nominations. He said the SEC had assured him that anyone willing to file a nomination would be given an opportunity.“We have lodged a complaint with evidence showing how YSRCP candidates were not allowed to file nominations. articles.title: France in flames: JD Vance blames immigration as violent protests leave historic town hall in ruins
articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has launched a scathing attack on France’s immigration policies, blaming them for the country’s escalating unrest as violent
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has launched a scathing attack on France’s immigration policies, blaming them for the country’s escalating unrest as violent protests over education cuts, rising living costs and public services swept several cities. The demonstrations were marked by arson, looting and clashes with police, with a fire partially destroying the 143-year-old town hall in Limoges.Vance’s remarks follow an earlier intervention by US president Donald Trump, who also attributed the unrest to 'mass migration' and 'Islam', dismissing the protests’ stated concerns over school conditions.In a post on social media, Vance criticised Western governments’ approach to immigration, diversity and assimilation.“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen,” Vance said.“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn. And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” he added.Earlier, in a post on Truth Social, Trump had said, “What's happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration.”“This isn't about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” Trump added.The protests, which began in late September, initially centred on deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages and education spending cuts before widening into demonstrations against rising living costs, inequality and pressure on public services.Violence escalated on Saturday, with public buildings and businesses targeted in several cities. articles.title: Gwalior temple tragedy: CM Mohan Yadav orders removal of City SP, suspension of 8 others after 14 killed
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav on Sunday ordered the removal of Gwalior’s City SP and eight others over alleged negligence that left
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav on Sunday ordered the removal of Gwalior’s City SP and eight others over alleged negligence that left 14 dead and 28 injured as a truck rammed into the devotees in a temple.“Instructions have been issued to immediately remove the CSP from his post and suspend three station house officers, one traffic inspector, one head constable, and three constables,” Yadav said in a post on X.Around 1.30 am on Sunday, a truck, with a Punjab registration number, entered the prohibited zone near a slope on Chinor Road and ran over devotees outside the Sheetla Mata temple, in Gwalior district, eventually ramming into its entrance gate. 14 people were killed in the incident; 28 were injured, with seven in critical condition, officials said, as per PTI. Two police personnel were also among the injured.A wall of the temple reportedly collapsed under the impact of the collision.The impact caused a temple wall to collapse, trapping people beneath the debris. The bodies of the deceased and the injured were taken to various hospitals, including the trauma centre in Gwalior."The accident occurred because the truck entered a prohibited area," Yadav told reporters in Indore, PTI reported.The CM also ordered a detailed investigation into the incident to find those responsible and ensure strict action against the guilty."The safety of all citizens is paramount. To prevent the recurrence of such incidents in future, security arrangements will be reviewed and necessary steps taken. No negligence will be tolerated at any level in public safety," he said.Yadav announced compensation of Rs 4 lakh each for the families of the deceased and said the government would cover the medical expenses of those seriously injured.Those who sustained minor injuries would receive financial assistance of Rs 50,000 each, he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2026, activists spent 70 days perched in a 200-year-old Arizona tree to save it from a border wall; federal agents cleared the protest, and crews cut it down
articles.summary: A 200-year-old cottonwood tree known as the 'grandmother' in Arizona was cut down by federal agents as activists protested against the construction of a border wall. The protests highlight concerns about wildlife corridors and environmental impacts in the region.
articles.body: A 200-year-old cottonwood tree in Lochiel, Arizona, was cut down on 5 October 2026 after protesters occupied its branches for more than 70 days. The tree was locally known as the “grandmother” and became the focal point of protest against a project slated to run two 30-foot-high parallel walls through San Rafael Valley. According to The Guardian, more than 80 federal agents arrived at the private land that morning and removed the last person occupying the tree and prevented demonstrators from reaching it. An excavator was used by contractors from Fisher Sand & Gravel to push the cottonwood to the ground.Participants had taken turns occupying a platform high in the tree, while supporters gathered and prayed near the construction site. Even after the grandmother tree fell, the protest continued, driven by the efforts of demonstrators trying to delay the construction along the border. Prior to the destruction, another ancient cottonwood in the area was felled on 27 July earlier this year.The wildlife corridor at riskThe San Rafael Valley is a remote high-elevation grassland between the Patagonia and Huachuca mountains in southern Arizona. Its landscape forms a vital wildlife corridor bridging the habitats between the United States and Mexico, and is home to jaguars, ocelots, bears, beavers, and porcupines. The demonstration raises concern about constructing a wall through this landscape, which would hinder the movement of wildlife between the two countries.According to Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, cottonwoods are the hallmark of riparian forests, dependent on underground water, and represent an endangered ecosystem found across Arizona and the southwestern United States. Their removal would not only affect the landscape’s appearance but also completely eliminate the trees from an ecological setting that is already under pressure.Another pressing concern brought about by the border infrastructure is water consumption. To construct the wall, water would be required to facilitate the preparation of concrete, and this would undoubtedly strain the local water supplies. To add more context, in 2008, US Border Patrol estimated that constructing a smaller wall nearby could require as much as 710,000 gallons of water per mile. The wall is being built using steel panels set into trenches containing reinforcing steel and concrete. By early October, contractors had completed the secondary barrier along part of the private property where the protesters camped. As of October 2026, 88 miles of secondary wall had already been completed nationally, with another 444 miles under construction, according to the Department of Homeland Security.Arrests and the continuing oppositionThe removal of tree sitters did not end the demonstrations, as protests continued with non-violent resistance. Earlier, on 7 August, a woman had attached herself to a cement truck so as to delay the work, and witnesses and videos cited by The Guardian indicated that she was sprayed with mace by the agents and removed from the cement truck.Afterwards, she was held in custody, according to information submitted by the authorities to her lawyers. The demonstration gained support from environmentalist Julia Butterfly Hill, who spent two years in the late 1990s in a California redwood, and condemned the act as horrifying. Speaking on the experience, Butterfly Hill told the Guardian, “She’s a hero of the highest order.”On October 8, the dispute made its way into Congress; Arizona congresswoman Adelita Grijalva said she intended to introduce legislation revoking the Department of Homeland Security's authority to waive any and all laws in border infrastructure. The proposal was a response to concerns over the powers used to advance construction, although it had not yet changed the work taking place in Lochiel.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Percy the Park Keeper author Nick Butterworth inspires reading at school
articles.summary: Nick Butterworth, 80, says reading is like entering a different world, and "I just believe in libraries for school".
articles.body:
An award-winning children's author who said he could not read until the age of eight visited a school library to inspire children to take up reading.

Percy the Park Keeper creator Nick Butterworth, 80, had previously auctioned off artwork to raise money for a library at Lionwood Infant School in Norwich, Norfolk, a few years ago.

In his latest visit, he said: "I just believe in libraries for schools, so many schools have lost libraries, and so I wanted to support them."

Butterworth said they had transformed the "uninspiring room" into a room that "kids want to come in and immerse themselves in stories".

Speaking to BBC Look East, Butterworth said: "There is something very personal about stories to me - I couldn't read until I was 8/9, but my mum reading stories to me [got me] hooked on stories - I wasn't hooked on reading - I was hooked on stories.

"She read to me long after children are read to, and she read me things like Moby-Dick and Tom Brown's School Days, Alice in Wonderland, and I fell in love with the languages as well as the stories themselves.

"I love that business of opening the cover of a book like a door that you go through into another world - I mean that is Alice in Wonderland."

Butterworth said reading to children at a very young age helps build strong relationships with them as well as filling them up with curiosity about how the world works.

"I want to see children reading and being read to just for the pleasure of it," he said, adding that children will pick up the language skills through that.

"Stories take us to places that we wouldn't normally have access to, and we get to meet people through stories that we would never come across.

"People whose lives are very different to ours, some better off and some much worse off than us."

He said he wished people would read stories for longer than they did, and added: "[We] watch a film together but wouldn't it be nice to sit down as a family and read a chapter of a book every night."

Selene Sawyer, executive headteacher of Lionwood, said Butterworth had been a "key feature" in getting the library up and running.

She said he was instrumental in donating a range of books, reading with the children and donating his artwork for auction.

Sawyer said the library deliberately does not have any screens, adding: "There are so many opportunities for children to just pick up a phone or an iPad and read on that, but the importance of being able to take time and look and understand text in its purest form is the most important thing."

Reception teacher Maisie Potter has started to teach her class how to read and said she tries to use screens as little as possible.

"[Storytelling] really helps with their imagination, and a lot of children don't get the opportunity to go into a different world, and they don't get to see as much as a book can give you," she said.

"We try and read them stories that could take them to a different place that they might not be able to go or have access to."
